searchText: If we assume that, ideally, each 64 KiB contract has all of its code written sequentially on disk, then with `66,667` contracts read in a `200M gas` block (`200M / 3k`), we have a baseline of `66,667` random I/O lookups. Under the EIP-7870 baseline, that's `66,667 / 50,000 = 1.33s` worth of random IOPS. Then, at EIP-7870's sequential read rate of `500 MB/s ≈ 477 MiB/s`, loading `66,667 × 64 KiB = 4,166.7 MiB` takes another `4,166.7 / 477 = 8.74s` of sequential reads, for a total of approximately `1.33s + 8.74s = 10.07s` per block. If you instead assume a worse case where the 4 KiB chunks making up each contract are scattered across the disk and require a separate random I/O each, then you get `66,667 × (64 / 4) = 1,066,672` random I/Os. At `50k IOPS`, that's `1,066,672 / 50,000 = 21.33s`. Either way you cut it, it seems really problematic? If there's no objections, I'm happy to give DoSing Plataberget a go? For random reads the limiting factor is latency, not throughput, so 50k IOPS × 4K doesn't need to match the 500 MB/s sequential number. They measure different things. For example :https://download.semiconductor.samsung.com/resources/data-sheet/Samsung_SSD_870_EVO_Data_Sheet_Rev1.1_230509.pdf, samsung evo 870 does : * ~550 MB/s sequential reads * 4k random reads are 98k IOPS QD32 (~400 MB/s) and 13k IOPS QD1 (~53 MB/s). We have same drive but different throughput depending on access pattern. In https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7870, there is also "**at least**", and states : **Recommended: 4 TB NVMe M.2 drive**. NVMe disks have much higher throughput on both sequential and random reads. This is an example of NVMe disk (not the most recent one) : https://download.semiconductor.samsung.com/resources/data-sheet/samsung_nvme_ssd_990_evo_plus_datasheet_rev.1.0.pdf I think I read only part of the message. The concern is valid even with sequential minimum throughput, those numbers doesn't represent anyway NVMe IO performance. They are minimal numbers so we may need to increase them. The numbers on the EIP look more like SATA SSD numbers than a NVMe. I think we should update this. I may be missing some context here, but wouldn’t this change add a codesize field to the account, thereby increasing the size of the account object? That seems somewhat counterproductive in the context of increasing state gas costs under EIP-8037. If running 64 KB contracts is considered stable by Glamsterdam, why don’t we use that as the baseline and only account for the excess beyond that threshold if we decide to further increase the code size limit in subsequent forks? From my perspective, it would make more sense to defer code access fee accounting until we have Verkle trees. > add a codesize field to the account Not necessarily, by loading the account you already figure out the codesize implicitly, you don't need to know the size of the contract before you load the whole thing for gas accounting purposes, and as such an extra field should not be necessary? > until we have verkle trees Can you elaborate more on why verkle trees are relevant? On a side note: I thought verkle trees were abandoned because the proposed implementations rely on non PQ secure vector commitments, and current lattice/FRI based ones are quite nascent still? Gotcha, will take a look. > I see that described in Verkle, where fees are calculated per chunk rather than on the raw bytecode, this pricing method is superior to the current flat pricing model. I agree we should meter based on contract size limit, this is the aim of EIP-7907 as discussed above, its not necessary to involve verkle trees for this though. > I really didn't know that; so, are we still using MPT? As far as I know yes, I haven't seen much development or talk on verkle trees in years at this point, but maybe someone else can confirm they are essentially dead? Still MPT, binary trie is next rather than verkle but don't know when it will land. Code size is problem today, can change pricing with a change in storage, that doesn't help with the issue right now though > From my perspective, it would make more sense to defer code access fee accounting until we have Verkle trees. Then we are blocked on gaslimit with 200M blocks as ceiling due to code sizes Or rather the "potential" worse case that you can load in blocks; even though that would never happen (unless it becomes an attack vector) Which is the wrong reason to cap something > Then we are blocked on gaslimit with 200M blocks as ceiling due to code sizes Charging for code access might be necessary, but why not also lower the costs for computational opcodes? I dislike inflating block limit just to present favorable metrics to users, when they are the ones ultimately paying the higher price for it. If the goal is to increase throughput for a specific resource, simply lower the cost associated with it. If code size is the limiting factor, upping gas limit and increasing cost for that specific resource will have the same effect as lowering costs for all other resources, all other things being equal. The issue is charging same for 448MB of code loading as 3.5GB of code loading, not sure how making opcodes cheaper helps with that? Changing every single parameter is much more complicated and harder to test than just changing 1 And if we can do 58K of 64kB contracts; shouldn't we allow 154K of 24KB contracts?

excerpts.author: sanleo
excerpts.content:
If we assume that, ideally, each 64 KiB contract has all of its code written sequentially on disk, then with `66,667` contracts read in a `200M gas` block (`200M / 3k`), we have a baseline of `66,667` random I/O lookups.

Under the EIP-7870 baseline, that's `66,667 / 50,000 = 1.33s` worth of random IOPS.

Then, at EIP-7870's sequential read rate of `500 MB/s ≈ 477 MiB/s`, loading `66,667 × 64 KiB = 4,166.7 MiB` takes another `4,166.7 / 477 = 8.74s` of sequential reads, for a total of approximately `1.33s + 8.74s = 10.07s` per block.

If you instead assume a worse case where the 4 KiB chunks making up each contract are scattered across the disk and require a separate random I/O each, then you get `66,667 × (64 / 4) = 1,066,672` random I/Os. At `50k IOPS`, that's `1,066,672 / 50,000 = 21.33s`.

Either way you cut it, it seems really problematic?

If there's no objections, I'm happy to give DoSing Plataberget a go?

excerpts.author: ahamlat
excerpts.content:
For random reads the limiting factor is latency, not throughput, so 50k IOPS × 4K doesn't need to match the 500 MB/s sequential number. They measure different things. For example :https://download.semiconductor.samsung.com/resources/data-sheet/Samsung_SSD_870_EVO_Data_Sheet_Rev1.1_230509.pdf, samsung evo 870 does :
* ~550 MB/s sequential reads 
* 4k random reads are 98k IOPS  QD32 (~400 MB/s) and 13k IOPS QD1 (~53 MB/s). 
We have same drive but different throughput depending on access pattern.
In https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7870, there is also "**at least**", and states : **Recommended: 4 TB NVMe M.2 drive**. NVMe disks have much higher throughput on both sequential and random reads. This is an example of NVMe disk (not the most recent one) : https://download.semiconductor.samsung.com/resources/data-sheet/samsung_nvme_ssd_990_evo_plus_datasheet_rev.1.0.pdf

excerpts.author: ahamlat
excerpts.content: I think I read only part of the message. The concern is valid even with sequential minimum throughput, those numbers doesn't represent anyway NVMe IO performance. They are minimal numbers so we may need to increase them.

excerpts.author: skylenet
excerpts.content: The numbers on the EIP look more like SATA SSD numbers than a NVMe. I think we should update this.

excerpts.author: gaxanh
excerpts.content:
I may be missing some context here, but wouldn’t this change add a codesize field to the account, thereby increasing the size of the account object? That seems somewhat counterproductive in the context of increasing state gas costs under EIP-8037.

If running 64 KB contracts is considered stable by Glamsterdam, why don’t we use that as the baseline and only account for the excess beyond that threshold if we decide to further increase the code size limit in subsequent forks?

From my perspective, it would make more sense to defer code access fee accounting until we have Verkle trees.

excerpts.author: sanleo
excerpts.content:
> add a codesize field to the account
Not necessarily, by loading the account you already figure out the codesize implicitly, you don't need to know the size of the contract before you load the whole thing for gas accounting purposes, and as such an extra field should not be necessary?

> until we have verkle trees
Can you elaborate more on why verkle trees are relevant?
On a side note: I thought verkle trees were abandoned because the proposed implementations rely on non PQ secure vector commitments, and current lattice/FRI based ones are quite nascent still? So seems quite far away.

excerpts.author: gaxanh
excerpts.content:
> and as such an extra field should not be necessary?
I see that it is written that way in the newly updated spec.

> Can you elaborate more on why verkle trees are relevant?
I see that described in Verkle, where fees are calculated per chunk rather than on the raw bytecode, this pricing method is superior to the current flat pricing model.

> I thought verkle trees were abandoned
I really didn't know that; so, are we still using MPT?

excerpts.author: sanleo
excerpts.content:
> I see that it is written that way in the newly updated spec.
Gotcha, will take a look.

> I see that described in Verkle, where fees are calculated per chunk rather than on the raw bytecode, this pricing method is superior to the current flat pricing model.
I agree we should meter based on contract size limit, this is the aim of EIP-7907 as discussed above, its not necessary to involve verkle trees for this though.

> I really didn't know that; so, are we still using MPT?
As far as I know yes, I haven't seen much development or talk on verkle trees in years at this point, but maybe someone else can confirm they are essentially dead?
